item.title: “Dutch directness was a relief, and a kind of healing”
item.description:
“Dutch directness was a relief, and a kind of healing”

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Elena Melkumova was head of education at a contemporary art museum in Moscow when a 2016 conference trip persuaded her to study museology in Amsterdam. She came back in 2022 and, after three years in the lighting industry, now creates educational programmes for lighting designers while working as an independent curator. She finds Dutch directness a relief and recommends a 12km walk through the dunes to the sea.

How did you end up in the Netherlands?
In 2016 I was head of education at Garage Museum of Contemporary Art in Moscow, and I was invited to an International Council of Museums conference on exchange between Dutch and Russian museum professionals. I fell for the country almost immediately: the professional community, the way people talked about culture, the networking. After the first day of the conference I called my mother and told her I wanted to study here.

So I ended up doing my master’s degree in museology at the Reinwardt Academie of the AHK. It was quite a spontaneous move. In 2022 I came back to Amsterdam, without any proper plan, because of the geopolitical situation. Since then my path has taken an unexpected turn. For three years I left museums for the lighting industry, but now I am slowly but surely coming back to the cultural field.

Today I combine the two worlds: I create educational programmes for lighting designers, and as an independent curator I still make exhibitions, most recently at the National Gallery of Armenia, with a Dutch artist among the participants. I hope to bring this exhibition to the Netherlands soon as well.

How do you describe yourself: expat, lovepat, immigrant, international?
In 2016 I felt 100% international, as I came because I had fallen in love with a professional culture. When I moved in 2022, I felt more like an immigrant at first, as I was genuinely puzzled about what to do and how to define myself. Now I feel international again. My work has always moved between countries, and that in-between position is where I am most at home.

How long do you plan to stay?
Each winter I have a different answer to that. Maybe I need to plan more of my holidays for the winter, and that will change. Last year I spent the winter in Portugal, and it was amazing. But coming back to the question: if I am honest, I have stopped answering that with a number. The Netherlands has shaped how I work and who I am now, and that stays with me wherever I am.

Do you speak Dutch and how did you learn?
By now my Dutch is good enough to follow work meetings, but not good enough to stop everyone at the bakery from switching to English. Strangely, the more I understand, the higher the barrier to speaking seems to get. I just need to push through it. Combining serious study with a full-time job and freelance work has been a challenge, but I have promised myself that next year I will get serious about learning and practising.

What’s your favourite Dutch thing?
Directness. I come from a culture where reading between the lines is perhaps too common a skill. In a Dutch workplace, when your manager says something, that is what they mean, and you do not have to spend the evening decoding it. For me that was a relief, and honestly a kind of healing.

How Dutch have you become?
I think I have become more direct and much more functional. I now judge things, from a bicycle to an exhibition layout, first by whether they work.

Which three Dutch people (dead or alive) would you most like to meet?
Bas Jan Ader, the conceptual artist who vanished at sea in 1975 while attempting to cross the Atlantic in a tiny boat, as part of his work In Search of the Miraculous. I would like to ask him what he was looking for.

Karel Martens, who makes his prints with found objects on an old letterpress. I would like to know how he has kept playing for sixty years.

And Robby Müller, the cinematographer who often worked only with natural or found light. I would like to ask him what he looked for first when he walked into a room.

What’s your top tourist tip?
Take a train, leave the city and get lost in the dunes somewhere by the sea. My favourite long walk: take the train to Overveen and cross the dunes to the Parnassia aan Zee beach pavillion, looking out for all the animals on the way. Stop there for a soda or an ice cream and maybe a dip in the sea, then walk on to Bloemendaal aan Zee and have mussels for lunch at one of the lovely beach bars with a view.

Then slowly but surely carry on to Zandvoort aan Zee and take the train back to the city. It is an easy 12 km walk. But if the weather is not great (so, half of the year, haha), I would recommend spending half a day at the Eye Filmmuseum: first see the current temporary exhibition, then have a quick lunch at the café overlooking the IJ, and finally watch one of the classics on 35mm.

Tell us something surprising you’ve found out about the Netherlands.
I was stunned at the beginning, and I am still amazed by how physically active people are here. People in this country spend so much time outside cycling, walking, exercising and even swimming, and I have adopted that 100%.

If you had just 24 hours left in the Netherlands, what would you do?
I would take my dog for a long early-morning walk in the Amsterdamse Bos. Then I would pay a short visit to the Stedelijk or the Rijksmuseum to see a few of my favourite pieces. After that I would have lunch with friends somewhere on a terrace.

Then I would take a train to the sea for a relaxed walk in the dunes and eat some oysters on the beach. Back in the city, I would use my Cineville card in the evening to see a great film at a cosy neighbourhood cinema, preferably LAB111 in Amsterdam, my all-time favourite.

Elena was talking with Louis Gore-Langton

item.title: Coalition on knife edge as VVD weighs response to tax deal
item.description:
Coalition on knife edge as VVD weighs response to tax deal

November 12, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The future of the coalition government is hanging by a thread after ruling parties centrist D66 and the Christian Democrat CDA struck a tax deal with two opposition parties on Wednesday, despite staunch objections from their coalition partner, the right-wing liberal VVD.

VVD leader Dilan Yesilgöz told reporters on Wednesday evening that the deal breached the coalition agreement, and that she wanted talks on a “fundamental reset” if D66 and the CDA went ahead with it.

According to broadcaster NOS, D66 and the CDA will vote for the amendment agreed with left-wing Pro and pro-European party Volt, regardless of what the VVD decides. The amendment will raise taxes on the very wealthy to cut the lowest rate of income tax.

The VVD had said it was “unthinkable” it could vote for the amendment in its original form, with MP Wendy van Eijk calling it “bad for the Netherlands”.

Yesilgöz said the new, watered-down version was still “a bad deal”, and that the VVD had been “caught off guard”. “Of course, if D66 and CDA would rather have a coalition agreement with Pro, then just say it,” she said.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten pulled out of an EU meeting in Dublin to attend Thursday’s debate on the tax plan, which starts at 10.15am Thursday.

The amendment D66 and the CDA agreed with Pro and Volt is a watered-down version of a “millionaires’ tax”. It would raise €1 billion, down from €1.5 billion in Pro and Volt’s original plan. It adds a new top rate of 38.5% in box 3, the tax on savings and investments. The money will go towards cutting the lowest rate of income tax.

Pro leader Jesse Klaver said the VVD was not involved in the negotiations. CDA leader Henri Bontenbal said the VVD had been kept informed “at several moments”.

Parliament backed a motion on Tuesday saying that if a cabinet collapses mid-term, MPs should first discuss forming a new coalition before new elections are called. Only one Dutch cabinet since 2000 has survived its full four-year term.

item.title: D66 and CDA agree deal with Pro to save budget, VVD frozen out
item.description:
D66 and CDA agree deal with Pro to save budget, VVD frozen out

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Coalition parties D66 and CDA have agreed an eleventh-hour deal with the left-wing Pro to break the deadlock in the Dutch budget talks.

The opposition party announced an amendment to raise an extra €1 billion in taxes on assets and savings, shortly after a 2pm deadline for changes to the cabinet’s tax plan expired.

The third party in the minority government, the right-wing liberal VVD, is expected to vote against the amendment, but enough minor parties are likely to support it to ensure a majority in the Lower House.

Prime minister Rob Jetten has cancelled a trip to Dublin for an EU leaders’ summit so he can attend an extra debate on the budget scheduled for Thursday morning.

The VVD has not responded to the announcement on the deal, but will now have to decided whether to accept the amended budget or withdraw its support altogether, which would trigger a cabinet collapse.

The amendment is a watered-down version of the original plan, tabled by Pro and pro-European party Volt, to raise an extra €1.5 billion by creating a new top tax rate for savers and investors with assets of more than €1.3 million. D66 and CDA described that proposal as “too coarse”.

The updated version will also bring an increase in tax on inheritance and cash gifts, and a pledge to crack down on tax avoidance schemes.

Millionaires’ tax

“This is a breakthrough,” said Pro party leader Jesse Klaver. “In the last few days we have held talks to bring about a compromise to make the Netherlands fairer. If this plan is accepted, the Netherlands will have a millionaires’ tax.”

The VVD was not involved in the negotiations, Klaver added. “We have talked to D66 and CDA. If you want to know if the VVD support it, you’ll have to ask them.”

Earlier the VVD said it was “unthinkable” it could vote for the amendment in its original form, with MP Wendy van Eijk saying the plan crossed her party’s “pain threshold” and was “bad for the Netherlands”.

Now the deadline to submit amendments has passed, the VVD will have to decide whether it can still support the budget with the wealth tax included. If not, it will mean the end of the coalition.

On Tuesday parliament voted for a motion calling on the cabinet to explore alternative coalitions before it decides to call early elections, in an attempt to prevent the third general election in just over three years.

If an election is called, it is expected to take place in March. In the meantime a caretaker government would have to try to cobble together a majority in parliament for a new budget plan.

item.title: Tilburg parties fear local arms deal could supply Israeli army
item.description:
Tilburg parties fear local arms deal could supply Israeli army

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Dutch defence firm AIA has announced plans to manufacture Israeli-designed guns in Tilburg, prompting six local parties to ask whether the council can stop the weapons ending up with the Israeli army.

D66, PRO, Denk, the Party for the Animals (PvdD), the Socialist Party (SP), and local party VoorTilburg013 submitted written questions to the council’s executive, regional broadcaster Omroep Brabant reported on Tuesday.

The parties say ties with Israeli arms maker IWI are undesirable because of the war in Gaza and the situation in the West Bank. Five of the six also want to know whether AIA has permission to make weapons in Tilburg, whether it could be withdrawn, and whether IWI will continue to earn money from the guns.

AIA announced on Monday that it had bought the designs and know-how for two IWI weapons, the Arad 5 rifle and the Negev UX light machine gun, which it says are particularly useful for anti-drone warfare. Production will start in Tilburg before moving to a larger site in Overijssel.

The guns are intended for European countries and Nato partners. It is not clear whether they could also be sold to Israel.

AIA director Gerard Zondervan told broadcaster NOS the deal was “just a business transaction” and that the company had had no contact with the Dutch government about it.

In January, MPs adopted a motion calling on the government to phase out the Netherlands’ dependence on the Israeli arms industry.

It said the Netherlands had bought €2 billion worth of military equipment from Israeli firms in recent years, and that it was undesirable to depend on military industries “involved in war crimes”.

Less than two months later, MPs adopted another motion, from the orthodox Protestant SGP, asking the government to actively seek cooperation with Israel in developing a European air and missile defence system.

item.description:
Youth, 16, arrested for shooting of 19-year-old man in garden

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

A 16-year-old youth has been arrested after a 19-year-old man was shot dead while gardening in Schiedam.

The victim was attacked by three people as he tended the front garden of a house in Weverpad with two other people on Saturday afternoon. Both his companions were wounded in the incident, but their injuries are not life-threatening.

One was taken to hospital for treatment, while the other suffered minor injuries and fled the scene. He was arrested by police but has since been released and is not regarded as a suspect.

Police arrested the 16-year-old male youth in Capelle aan den IJssel on Tuesday afternoon on suspicion of murder or attempted murder. The search for the other two suspected assailants is ongoing.

The shooting may have been a case of mistaken identity, police said. A large-scale inquiry led by the prosecution service is ongoing.

The town’s mayor, Harold Bergmann, has placed security cameras outside the scene of the shooting and two nearby houses where explosions took place the following day. Police have not established if the incidents are linked.

item.title: NL and Germany sign deal on faster, more frequent trains
item.description:
NL and Germany sign deal on faster, more frequent trains

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Netherlands and Germany have agreed to increase the number of trains running between them and cut travel times, with a focus on shortening the route to Berlin.

Annet Bertram, junior minister for public transport and rail, signed a joint declaration with German transport minister Steffen Bilger in Berlin on Tuesday. The agreement covers cross-border passenger and freight traffic, including military transport.

Bertram, of the centrist Christian Democrat CDA, told broadcaster NOS that she had wanted to travel to Berlin by train, but that current diversions made it impossible. “That is exactly why it is important that we discuss these issues in Berlin now,” she said.

The two countries will improve the main border routes and give new rail operators more access to the network.

The journey from Amsterdam to Berlin, 660km, takes almost seven hours, compared with three and a half hours for the 500km trip to Paris, according to NOS.

National rail operator NS and Deutsche Bahn run just four direct trains to Berlin, and all of them will be cancelled for three months next spring because of engineering work.

“Interest is not the problem, speed is,” Bertram said. She told NOS she would like to see “several options an hour” to Berlin or Frankfurt within 10 to 15 years.

item.title: Court upholds licence for Amsterdam TikTok sensation Fabel Friet
item.description:
Court upholds licence for Amsterdam TikTok sensation Fabel Friet

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

Amsterdam city council was entitled to extend the licence for a chip shop whose long queues have been blamed by local residents for damaging the quality of life in the city centre neighbourhood, a court has ruled.

A judge said campaigners had failed to show that the problems were solely or mainly caused by customers of Fabel Friet, which has become a magnet for tourists drawn by the social media platform TikTok.

The decision is a setback for locals who wanted the court to overturn an extension to Fabel Friet’s licence, which was granted by the city council in 2024. The court was not asked to rule on the current licence issued this year.

They said the queues at the outlet in Runstraat, stretching back to the canal bridge, added to problems with overcrowding in the Negen Straatjes district  and attracted seagulls to the area.

“The number of places where they can sit and eat their chips without causing a nuisance is quite limited,” resident Niek van der Heijden told the court at an earlier hearing.

But judges said Fabel Friet was not primarily responsible for the queues and litter problems and the licence was granted correctly.

Exotic toppings

“Other catering outlets in the neighbourhood also attract large numbers of visitors and have queues,” the court said in a press release.

“The court concludes that it cannot be assumed that the problems experiences are solely or primarliy caused by customers of Fabel Friet. The neighbouring residents have not demonstrated this.”

Fabel Friet’s founders, Abel Klatzer and Floris Feilzer, have opened four other branches in the city centre since they launched the business in 2020, but the outlet in Runstraat remains their flagship.

Tourists flocked to the shop after their videos of their fries topped with exotic toppings such as Parmesan cheese and truffle mayonnaise were widely shared on TikTok.

The owners set up a special queueing system and hired extra security to try to keep order in the neighbourhood. At one stage they also employed a falconer to keep away the seagulls that ripped open the rubbish bags outside the shop and spilled the contents all over the street.

item.title: Johan Cruyff’s grandson called up to play for USA under-18 team
item.description:
Johan Cruyff’s grandson called up to play for USA under-18 team

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The most famous name in Dutch football could appear on an international men’s team sheet for the first time in 30 years after Johan Cruyff’s grandson was called up for the United States’ upcoming matches in Europe.

Shae Cruijff-Beane, the son of Johan Cruyff’s daughter Chantal and her American husband Todd Beane, was included in the squad that will play against Norway and Portugal in the next seven days.

Cruijff-Beane plays as a midfielder for Gimnàstic de Tarragona, a club in the Spanish third tier based near Barcelona. His older brother Jordan also came through the club’s ranks and is currently playing US college football at Westmont College in California.

Shae, 17, is eligible to play for the USA through his father and Spain and the Netherlands through his mother, who spent part of her childhood in Catalonia while Johan Cruyff was playing for Barcelona in the 1970s.

The USA under-18 squad also includes an Ajax player, midfielder Xander Newstead, who grew up in San Francisco and joined the Amsterdam club’s youth team set-up at the age of 10, beforec signing professional terms last year.

Johan Cruyff went on to play in the United States for Los Angeles Aztecs and Washington Diplomats before returning to the Netherlands, winding down his career at Ajax and Feyenoord.

His son Jordi played for Barcelona and Manchester United and won nine international caps in 1996. Last year he was appointed technical director at Ajax, the club where his father began his career.

item.title: What’s on at IDFA 2026: five documentaries to watch
item.description:
What’s on at IDFA 2026: five documentaries to watch

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The International Documentary Film Festival Amsterdam (IDFA) opens on Thursday for its 39th edition, with 253 films from 80 countries screening until November 22.

The festival was founded in 1988 by Ally Derks, at a time when documentaries rarely made it into Dutch cinemas. The first edition showed 72 films to around 2,000 visitors.

There are prizes for the best films in the International Competition and the Envision Competition, which is for more experimental work.

There are also prizes for the best debut, the best Dutch film and the best use of archive footage. The winners will be announced on November 19.

Here are some highlights to look out for:

White Tiger Column
The opening film follows a group of young recruits through 45 days of training at a jungle camp run by Myanmar’s resistance movement. Canadian directors Robert Mentov, Dwight Jantzi and Bryan Dickie filmed the volunteers’ daily routines as they prepare to fight. The film is in the International Competition and is also nominated for the award for best first feature.

You Can See Everything
Elizabeth Holmes, the founder of blood-testing company Theranos, invited comedian Nathan Fielder and director Lance Oppenheim into her home in the weeks before she went to prison. They filmed her daily life with her partner, hotel heir Billy Evans, and their two children. The film was made in secret from 2023 and unveiled at a surprise screening at the Telluride film festival in September.

Musk
Oscar winner Alex Gibney’s portrait of Elon Musk runs to almost four hours. Gibney expanded the film after Musk briefly became one of President Trump’s closest aides and set about cutting the federal government. The film premiered at the Venice film festival in September.

30 mei, 1969 (gritu di un pueblo)
On May 30, 1969, aworkers in Curaçao went on strike, which grew into a popular uprising against exploitation and inequality. The Dutch government sent troops to the island, causing political turmoil. Curaçao-born filmmaker John Leerdam made the film 25 years later, interviewing people who were involved and drawing on archive footage. It first screened at IDFA in 1995, and is returning this year in a new restoration by Amsterdam’s Eye Filmmuseum.

No Man’s Air
On July 20, 1974, the last flight landed at Nicosia Airport before Turkey invaded Cyprus. The airport has sat ever since in the no man’s land between the Greek and Turkish parts of the island. In this 42-minute film, Dutch filmmakers Peter Delpeut and Gerco de Ruijter use found footage to reconstruct that flight, with the Cypriot captain narrating off screen.

item.title: No sign of breakthrough as deadline looms on Dutch tax plans
item.description:
No sign of breakthrough as deadline looms on Dutch tax plans

November 11, 2026

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results

Add as a favourite source on Google Add DutchNews as a favourite source on Google

The Dutch government is running out of time to find a majority in parliament for its tax programme for next year, with no sign of a breakthrough in negotiations with opposition parties.

Prime minister Rob Jetten has repeatedly said he wants to secure a broad agreement with concessions on the left and right, but the two sides’ demands are proving irreconcilable.

Junior finance minister Eelco Eerenberg, who is responsible for the tax plans, called on MPs to “look with a clear head and a new day at what is on the table”, at the end of a debate that brought the parties no closer to ending the deadlock.

The minority coalition of D66, CDA and VVD need to find 10 votes in the lower house and 17 votes in the Senate from at least two opposition parties to pass their legislation.

The parties have until 2pm on Wednesday to table fresh amendments, after which the tax plans will go to a vote in the lower house, which is scheduled for Thursday. The Senate is due to vote in December.

The left-wing Pro, who have teamed up the pro-European liberal minor party Volt, are pressing the cabinet to raise another €1.5 billion in taxes on people with high levels of assets and savings to fund tax cuts for working people.

But the move is being blocked by the right-wing liberal VVD, who favour doing a deal instead with a right-wing block of JA21, the farmers’ party BBB and the orthodox Protestant SGP.

Split vote

The coalition parties have not ruled out splitting their vote on Pro’s amendement, an unprecedented move that would allow D66, CDA and Pro to pass the measure with support from other opposition groups while the VVD vote against.

The tax service has warned that if the plans are not passed before November 20 it will not be able to include the new rates in next year’s tax demands, meaning millions of taxpayers will be sent incorrect bills that have to be adjusted later.

Employers’ payslips will also be calculated on the basis of the 2026 rates for at least the first quarter.

With the prospect of a cabinet collapse looming, MPs backed a motion on Tuesday requiring parliament to explore alternative combinations before resorting to fresh elections.

The motion, tabled by the Christian parties ChristenUnie, SGP and CDA, would change the parliament’s procedural rules, to say MPs “will consult on a new formation” after a cabinet resigns rather than “can consult”.

Only one of the last seven Dutch governments has lasted the full term and a general election in March 2027, the earliest it could be held, would be the third in less than three and a half years.
